entries.topic: Health costs and coverage: wartime origin of employer insurance, spending vs outcomes, premiums, uninsured and underinsured, 2025 law Medicaid changes

claims.text: KFF EHBS 2026 (published 22 Oct 2026): average family premium $28,303 (+~5%), single $9,804; worker contribution for family $7,471 (+$621), i.e. 27% of family premium, 18% of single; average single deductible $1,955; 38% of covered workers have single deductible >= $2,000 (34% in 2025); 29% in HSA-qualified plans; 67% of firms with 10+ workers offer health benefits; over five years family premiums +28% vs wages +26.9% and inflation +24.4%; workers in firms with many lower-wage workers contribute 31% vs 27%; 7% of large firms said services subject to prior authorization rose
KFF 2021: average family premium $22,221 (+4%), worker contribution $5,969; single deductible $1,669 vs $991 in 2011; family premiums +47% since 2011
KFF 2016: average family premium $18,142, worker contribution $5,277; 20% above 2011 and 58% above 2006
KFF 2011: family premium $15,073 (+9%); workers pay $4,129, employers $10,944; family premiums +113% since 2001 vs workers' wages +34% and inflation +27%
KFF 2020: average family premium $21,342, single $7,470

Thomasson (2017 testimony): National War Labor Board wage limits from 1942 exempted health insurance and other fringe benefits, so firms used benefits to attract scarce workers; first tax exclusion of employer-paid premiums came under a narrow 1943 administrative ruling, later codified in the 1954 Internal Revenue Code; roughly 9% of Americans had hospital insurance by 1940 and about 50% by 1950; the 1954 statute increased the generosity of plans and the number of firms offering coverage
Thomasson (AER 2003): the 1954 tax subsidy increased the growth of group insurance, particularly among union members and employed persons

Tax Policy Center: the exclusion for employer-sponsored insurance was estimated to cost $299bn in income and payroll taxes in 2022, the single largest tax expenditure; it is worth more in higher brackets: a $1,000 premium saves $254 in the 12% bracket and $347 in the 22% bracket (income plus payroll tax)

WHO/World Bank current health expenditure per capita, PPP, United States: 2000 4,549; 2005 6,429; 2010 7,836; 2015 9,201; 2019 10,550; 2020 11,648; 2021 12,080; 2022 12,586; 2023 13,473 (current international $)

Commonwealth Fund 2026 (2024 data): US health spending 18% of GDP, nearly twice the OECD average; per capita 1.5 times Switzerland (next highest); US life expectancy 79 years, two years below OECD average; second-highest avoidable mortality among included countries (after Mexico); maternal deaths nearly 19 per 100,000 live births (2023) vs under 5 in 11 of 18 countries; fewest primary care physicians per capita; average out-of-pocket drug spending over $400 vs under $100 in France; US and Mexico the only countries without universal coverage

Commonwealth Fund 2024 Biennial Survey (March-June 2024, 6,480 adults 19-64): 56% adequately insured all year; 23% insured all year but underinsured (out-of-pocket costs excl. premiums >=10% of income, or >=5% if under 200% FPL, or deductible >=5% of income); 12% had a coverage gap; 9% uninsured; 66% of underinsured had employer coverage; about 3 in 10 paying off medical debt; 44% of underinsured reported medical or dental debt

CMS: Medicare and Medicaid signed by President Lyndon B. Johnson on 30 July 1965; Medicare extended to disabled and ESRD in 1972; CHIP created 1997; Part D added by MMA 2003, effective 2006; ACA 2010 created the Marketplace

KFF on CBO estimates for the 2025 reconciliation law (signed 4 July 2025): federal health spending reduced by over $1tn; work requirements (Sec. 71119) -$326bn federal Medicaid over 10 years, +5.3m uninsured in 2034; provider taxes -$191bn, +1.1m; state-directed payments -$149bn; six-month redeterminations for expansion adults from renewals on/after 31 Dec 2026, -$63bn, +0.7m; cost sharing up to $35 per service for expansion adults 100-138% FPL from 1 Oct 2028

Georgetown CCF: CMS-2454-IFC interim final rule published June 2026 implements Medicaid work/community engagement requirements: expansion adults 19-64, 80 hours/month of work, community service, work programme or half-time education (or income >= $580/month), from 1 Jan 2027; law allows good-faith exemptions to 31 Dec 2028 but IFR limits initial exemption to six months; exclusions include parents of children 13 or younger, medically frail, pregnant/postpartum, AI/AN, disabled veterans; Nebraska already implementing

ASTHO: enhanced premium tax credits (from 2021) expired end-2025; House passed HR 1834 three-year extension 230-196 on 8 Jan 2026; Senate efforts failed or stalled; 2025 marketplace enrollment 24.3m (11.4m in 2020), 92% with enhanced credits
HFMA: 2026 open enrollment plan selections 23.1m, -4.9% from 24.3m in 2025; Congress did not extend enhanced subsidies
KFF Feb 2026: 2026 is first year since 2020 without enhanced PTCs; premium payments up about 114% on average for subsidized enrollees staying in the same plan

entries.topic: Claim denials, prior authorization, PBMs and hospital prices

claims.text: KFF (CMS transparency data, HealthCare.gov non-group QHPs, 2024): 19% of in-network claims denied (about 85m of 451m); out-of-network 37%; insurer in-network denial rates 3%-36%; denial reasons: other 36%, administrative 25%, excluded service 13%, lack of prior authorization/referral 9%, medical necessity 5%; at least 262,982 internal appeals (<1% of denials), 165,863 (66%) upheld; at least 5,881 external appeals; pre-service PA denials not included; data limitations

KFF: Medicare Advantage insurers made 52.8m prior authorization determinations in 2024; 4.1m (7.7%) denied fully or partly (6.4% in 2023); 11.5% of denials appealed; 80.7% of appeals fully or partly overturned; traditional Medicare 628,243 reviews FY2024, 22.9% denied; CMS 2024 rule: 7-day standard decisions from Jan 2026, APIs Jan 2027; WISeR model from 1 Jan 2026 adds prior authorization to traditional Medicare in six states (NJ, OH, OK, TX, AZ, WA)

23 June 2025: HHS Secretary Kennedy and CMS Administrator Oz announced an insurer pledge (AHIP, BCBSA, 12 companies incl. Aetna, Kaiser, UnitedHealthcare) covering 257m people: demonstrated reductions in services subject to PA by 1 Jan 2026; 90-day continuity for plan switchers; 80% of electronic PA approvals answered in real time by 2027; standard electronic framework by 1 Jan 2027

BCBSA: prior authorization intended to 'ensure patients receive care that is safe, evidence-based and as affordable as possible'; first commitments took effect 1 Jan 2026; plans serving nearly 270m participating

FTC interim staff report (9 July 2024, 4-1 vote; Holyoak dissent, Ferguson caution): top three PBMs processed nearly 80% of about 6.6bn prescriptions in 2023, top six more than 90%; affiliated pharmacies of the top three nearly 70% of specialty drug revenue; affiliated pharmacies paid 20-40x NADAC for two specialty generics

FTC second interim report (14 Jan 2025): PBM-affiliated pharmacies of Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx earned $7.3bn above estimated acquisition cost on specialty generics 2017-2022; $1.4bn more from spread pricing; plan sponsors paid $4.8bn and patients $297m cost sharing for these drugs in 2021

FTC second report: 63% of specialty generics dispensed by the big PBMs' affiliated pharmacies 2020-2022 marked up 100%+ over NADAC, 22% marked up 1,000%+; PCMA spokesman called the report unlikely to be more than advocacy and said PBMs are 'the only entities in the supply chain dedicated to lowering the cost of prescription drugs'

FTC insulin case (Docket 9437) against Caremark, Express Scripts, OptumRx and their GPOs alleges rebating practices inflated insulin list prices; Express Scripts settled 4 Feb 2026, FTC expects up to $7bn lower patient costs over 10 years; case page lists status pending
FTC press release 14 July 2026: settlement with Caremark resolving antitrust case against second drug middleman

BenefitsPRO 16 June 2026: Optum Rx reached a proposed settlement (terms undisclosed) and the case was withdrawn from adjudication pending FTC review; all three PBMs denied the allegations; ESI terms include delinking compensation from negotiated savings and moving GPO Ascent from Switzerland to US; complaint filed fall 2024
Consolidated Appropriations Act 2026, signed 3 Feb 2026: Part D PBM compensation delinked from list prices and rebates (flat fees), 100% pass-through of rebates to payer, CMS reporting

CAA 2026 ERISA provisions: PBMs must pass through 100% of rebates and fees to employer plans and report compensation; effective about 30 months after enactment; Medicare reforms generally from 1 Jan 2028

RAND (round 5): employers and private insurers paid hospitals 254% of Medicare rates in 2022 (224% in 2020, 247% in 2018); above 300% in CA, FL, GA, NY, SC, WV, WI; below 200% in AR, IA, MA, MI, MS; AHA called it skewed and incomplete, covering under 2% of hospital spending

entries.topic: Medical debt totals, bankruptcy dispute, credit reporting rules and state laws, medical credit cards

claims.text: CFPB (1 March 2022): estimated $88bn in medical bills on credit reports; as of Q2 2021, 58% of bills in collections on credit records are medical; medical collections tradelines on 43m credit reports; roughly 20% of households report medical debt; medical collections less predictive of repayment; past-due medical debt Black 28%, Hispanic 22%, white 17%, Asian 10%; more common in the Southeast and Southwest, partly because states there did not expand Medicaid

Credit bureaus (18 March 2022): paid medical collections removed from 1 July 2022; wait before unpaid medical collections appear extended from 6 months to one year; medical collections under $500 removed in first half of 2023; together nearly 70% of medical collection tradelines removed

AP: Judge Sean Jordan (E.D. Tex.) struck down the CFPB medical-debt credit-report rule on 11 July 2025 as exceeding CFPB authority under the FCRA; CFPB had estimated the rule would remove $49bn in medical debt from 15m Americans' reports and raise scores by about 20 points on average

NCLC (updated 21 Sept 2026): rule vacated 11 July 2025 in Cornerstone Credit Union League v. CFPB (challenged with CDIA); CFPB interpretive rule 28 Oct 2025 (90 FR 48710) states FCRA preempts state laws on report contents, while saying it is not binding and courts decide; 15 states plus DC restrict medical debt on credit reports: CA, CO, CT, DE, DC (Aug 2026), IL, ME, MD, MN, NJ, NY, OR, RI, VT, VA, WA

KFF Health Care Debt Survey (Feb-Mar 2022, published 16 June 2022): 41% of adults currently have debt from medical or dental bills (broad definition incl. payment plans, credit card balances, loans from family); 63% of them cut back on food, clothing or household items; 44% owe $2,500+, 12% $10,000+; 18% think they will never pay it off

CFPB (via KFF Health News, May 2023): people paid about $1bn in deferred interest on medical credit cards and other medical financing 2018-2020; rates up to 27%; deferred interest can raise bills by almost 25%; CFPB in 2013 ordered CareCredit (Synchrony) to set up a $34.1m reimbursement fund

KFF Health News 'Diagnosis: Debt': 'More than 100 million people in America - a startling 41% of adults' have medical bills they cannot pay; the project lists the KFF Health Care Debt Survey (Feb-Mar 2022, 2,375 adults) among its data sources

entries.topic: Audit corrections and status checks, Part Eight

claims.text: KFF EHBS 2026: average single deductible $1,955 is for covered workers in plans with a general annual deductible; firms where at least 35% of workers earn $38,000 or less have a family contribution rate of 31% vs 27% at other firms; workers contribute an average $7,471, about 27% of the family premium
Commonwealth Fund 2024 survey: people in employer plans and in the individual market and marketplaces reported significantly higher rates of medical debt than people with Medicaid

As of its 21 October 2026 update: the enhanced ACA premium tax credits expired at the end of 2025 and Congress had not passed an extension for 2027; without action the original eligibility rules apply in 2027

As of 5 October 2026 the Medicaid work requirement start of 1 January 2027 had not been delayed; five governors asked HHS to use enforcement discretion to delay compliance until states can demonstrate readiness, without proposing a replacement date; no HHS decision reported
FTC announced a proposed settlement with Optum Rx on 12 June 2026; as of 20 July 2026 the specific terms had not been publicly released
